refined_brief: Source-grounded 4:3 black/white abstracts with framed subfigures, appropriate quantitative plots, explained terminology, consistent spacing and right-aligned source credits.
central_argument: Situated context prompts the user to recall an association before SnapTag offers the answer, preserving agency in everyday memory support.
source_evidence: Paper pages 138-140. Scenario 1 names Veena Malik, age 62, a homemaker leaving home to visit a neighbor: she tags keys and spectacles and associates them with the doorway. A contextual prompt first shows the tags; tapping reveals the object identity, with an optional camera aid if it is still not located. Scenario 2 names Ramesh Pai, age 68: photographs/color associations connect medicines to the cabinet and time after lunch. The study involved five adults ages 58-70, using interviews, routine mapping and shadowing; prototype feedback reported a sense of accomplishment and acknowledgment of effort.
limitations: The person is an illustrative reconstruction of the published scenario character, not a portrait of an actual participant. Sari clothing is an illustrative choice, not a documented study attribute. Only shape cues are retained for the monochrome tag associations. The medicine sequence is schematic and provides no dosing instruction. No measured long-term self-efficacy gain or clinical benefit is claimed. The original prototype and raw participant data are unavailable.
